entries.meaning: To cover something with a protective layer of metal or other hard material. ---
examples: The company armors trucks for use in war zones.
They armored the embassy doors after the attack.
Every vehicle in the convoy has been armored.
entries.contrast: American English spells it armor, armored, armoring; British English writes armour, armoured, armouring.

entries.meaning: To stir up a feeling or reaction in someone. ---
examples: Questions like that arouse suspicion immediately.
His sudden wealth aroused the interest of the tax office.
The story has aroused strong feelings on both sides.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse arouse, which is regular (aroused, aroused), with arise, which is irregular (arose, arisen).

entries.meaning: To bring someone before a court to hear the charges and answer them. ---
examples: Prosecutors will arraign the suspect on Monday morning.
She was arraigned on three counts of fraud.
The court has arraigned all four defendants.
entries.русский: предъявлять обвинение в суде, привлекать к суду
entries.contrast: The g is silent: arraign is uh-RAYN. You are arraigned on a charge.

entries.meaning: To find something out for certain by checking the facts. ---
examples: We need to ascertain who was in the building that night.
Investigators ascertained the cause of the fire within a week.
The police have not yet ascertained how the thieves got in.

entries.meaning: To kill or be killed by a lack of oxygen. ---
examples: Carbon monoxide can asphyxiate a person in minutes.
Two workers were asphyxiated by fumes inside the tank.
The gas was slowly asphyxiating everyone in the basement.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the fumes asphyxiated two workers), intransitive (the miners asphyxiated underground)

entries.meaning: To have a strong desire to reach something important. ---
examples: Many of these students aspire to a career in medicine.
She aspired to be the first in her family to finish college.
He has always aspired to something bigger than this town.
entries.contrast: aspire takes to: aspire to a position, aspire to be something. Never "aspire for".

entries.meaning: To attack someone or something violently, with blows or with words. ---
examples: Critics assail the mayor every time the budget comes up.
Reporters assailed the senator with questions about the leak.
The coast has been assailed by three storms this month.

entries.meaning: To state something firmly as true, or to claim a right with confidence. ---
examples: The report asserts that the numbers were changed on purpose.
She asserted her right to speak to a lawyer.
He has asserted his innocence from the very first day.

entries.meaning: To take something in and absorb it fully, or to become part of a larger group. ---
examples: It takes weeks to assimilate this much new material.
Her grandparents assimilated within a few years of arriving.
The team is still assimilating the data from last season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (assimilate new information), intransitive (the family assimilated quickly)

entries.meaning: To shock someone with surprise or amazement. ---
examples: The size of the crowd will astound you.
His answer astounded the whole committee.
We were astounded by how quickly the work was finished.

entries.meaning: To make up for something wrong that you have done. ---
examples: Nothing he does now can atone for that decision.
She atoned for the mistake by working through the weekend.
He has spent years atoning for the harm he caused.
entries.contrast: atone takes for: atone for a mistake, never "atone a mistake".

entries.meaning: To waste away and grow weak from lack of use. ---
examples: Muscles atrophy quickly when a leg is in a cast.
His Russian atrophied after ten years away from home.
The program has atrophied since the funding was cut.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (weeks in bed atrophy the muscles), intransitive (the muscles atrophy)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: atrophies, atrophied, but the -ing form keeps it: atrophying.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something sensitive and well adjusted to something. ---
examples: Years in the classroom attune a teacher to small changes in mood.
The training attuned the staff to the needs of older customers.
She is well attuned to what her readers want.
entries.contrast: Almost always used with to: attuned to the market. American English says uh-TOON, not "uh-TYOON".

entries.meaning: To make something larger or stronger by adding to it. ---
examples: Many teachers augment their income with summer work.
The city augmented the police budget after the vote.
The library has augmented its collection with three thousand new titles.

entries.meaning: To be a sign of how something is going to turn out. ---
examples: Weak sales augur badly for the holiday season.
The early numbers augured well for the new director.
Nothing in that first meeting augured the trouble that followed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the result augurs a difficult year), intransitive (this augurs well for the talks)
entries.contrast: Do not confuse augur, to foretell, with auger, a tool for drilling holes; both are said AW-gur.

entries.meaning: To write a book, a report, or a piece of legislation. ---
examples: Two economists author the annual report together.
She authored the bill that became law last spring.
He has authored more than a dozen novels.

entries.meaning: To change a typed word automatically to the one the software thinks you meant. ---
examples: My phone always autocorrects his name to something else.
The app autocorrected "definitely" to "defiantly".
I sent the text without noticing that it had autocorrected the address.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the phone autocorrected my message), intransitive (the field autocorrects as you type)

entries.meaning: To wait for something that is expected. ---
examples: Three more patients await their test results.
We awaited the verdict in complete silence.
He is awaiting trial in a county jail.
entries.contrast: await takes a direct object with no preposition: await a decision, but wait for a decision.

entries.meaning: To wake up, or to wake someone else up, used of feelings as well as of sleep. ---
examples: One phone call can awaken the whole house.
The smell of coffee awakened something like hope in him.
She had awakened long before the alarm went off.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the noise awakened the baby), intransitive (she awakened at dawn)
entries.contrast: awaken is regular: awakened, awakened. It is awake that is irregular: awoke, awoken.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with a feeling of wonder and deep respect. ---
examples: The scale of the canyon awes almost every visitor.
We were awed by the silence inside the cathedral.
Her performance has awed critics across the country.
entries.contrast: The silent e drops before -ing: awe → awing.

entries.meaning: To get rid of something suddenly, such as a job, a show, or a budget line. ---
examples: The network may axe the show after one season.
The company axed four hundred jobs in a single morning.
Three of the projects have already been axed.
entries.contrast: American English also spells it ax; both spellings give axed and axing.

entries.meaning: To talk quickly and foolishly, or to make a soft running sound like a stream. ---
examples: The twins babble to each other for hours.
He babbled something about missing his flight.
A little stream was babbling just beyond the trees.

entries.meaning: To treat someone with far too much care and protection. ---
examples: Don't baby him — he can carry his own bag.
His mother babied him well into his twenties.
You are babying that car; it will be fine on gravel.
entries.русский: нянчиться, баловать, обращаться как с ребёнком
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: babies, babied, but the -ing form keeps it: babying.

entries.meaning: To put an earlier date on a document or a payment than the real one. ---
examples: The contract lets the company backdate the raise to January.
Someone had backdated the invoices by six months.
Executives were accused of backdating their stock options.

entries.meaning: To produce the opposite of the result that was intended. ---
examples: Threats like that usually backfire.
The ad campaign backfired badly.
Their attempt to bury the story has backfired on them.

entries.meaning: To go back the way you came, or to take back something you said earlier. ---
examples: Let me backtrack a little and explain that first step again.
The governor backtracked within hours of the interview.
He has been backtracking on that promise all week.
entries.русский: идти на попятную, отступать от сказанного; возвращаться тем же путём

entries.meaning: To put food on a hook or in a trap, or to provoke someone on purpose. ---
examples: He baits the hook with a piece of shrimp.
She baited her brother until he lost his temper.
The traps had been baited the night before.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse bait with bate, which survives only in the phrase with bated breath.

entries.meaning: To refuse suddenly to do or accept something. ---
examples: Buyers balk at prices like that.
The board balked when it saw the final figure.
He is balking at signing anything before his lawyer reads it.
entries.contrast: balk takes at: balk at the cost. British English spells it baulk, and the l is silent either way: BAWK.

entries.meaning: To grow very quickly to a much larger size. ---
examples: Repair costs can balloon once the walls are opened up.
The deficit ballooned during the crisis.
Class sizes have ballooned since the two schools merged.

entries.meaning: To trick or thoroughly confuse someone, usually in order to get something. ---
examples: Salesmen like that bamboozle people every day.
He bamboozled his neighbors into lending him money.
We were completely bamboozled by the paperwork.

entries.meaning: To hit something hard, making a loud noise. ---
examples: Please don't bang the door when you leave.
She banged her knee on the table leg.
Someone has been banging on the pipes all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he banged the door), intransitive (someone was banging on the wall)

entries.meaning: To send someone away from a place as a punishment, or to drive a thought out of your mind. ---
examples: Old kings could banish anyone who displeased them.
He was banished from the country for twenty years.
She spent the whole flight banishing thoughts of the meeting.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: banishes.

entries.meaning: To put or keep money in a bank. ---
examples: Where do you bank?
He banked most of the prize money.
They have banked with the same branch for thirty years.
entries.русский: класть в банк, держать деньги в банке
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she banked the check), intransitive (we bank at a credit union)

entries.meaning: To leave a person or company with no money at all. ---
examples: One bad season can bankrupt a small farm.
The lawsuit nearly bankrupted the family.
Medical bills have bankrupted thousands of households.

entries.meaning: To admit someone into the Christian church in a ceremony using water. ---
examples: The priest will baptize the child on Sunday.
She was baptized in the same church as her mother.
He has baptized three generations of that family.
entries.contrast: American English spells it baptize, baptized; British English usually writes baptise, baptised.

entries.meaning: To uncover something, or to reveal something private. ---
examples: The dog bares its teeth at strangers.
He bared his arm so the nurse could find a vein.
She has never bared that part of her life to anyone.
entries.contrast: bare sounds exactly like bear, the animal and the irregular verb bear, bore, borne. The silent e drops before -ing: baring.

entries.meaning: To block a road or a doorway with something heavy so that nobody can get through. ---
examples: Protesters barricade the main road every spring.
The gunman barricaded himself in the back office.
Both entrances had been barricaded with office furniture.

entries.meaning: To work as a bartender, serving drinks in a bar. ---
examples: She bartends three nights a week to pay for school.
He bartended at a hotel downtown all summer.
I have been bartending since I was twenty-one.

entries.meaning: To build something on a particular fact, idea, or place as its foundation. ---
examples: Scientists base that conclusion on thirty years of data.
The movie was based on a true story.
The company is basing its new office in Denver.
entries.contrast: base takes on: based on the evidence. It sounds like bass, the low voice.

entries.meaning: To hit something hard, or to attack someone harshly in words. ---
examples: Politicians bash each other for months before an election.
He bashed his elbow against the door frame.
The paper has been bashing the mayor all year.
entries.contrast: Ends in -sh, so the third person adds -es: bashes.

entries.meaning: To fight or struggle hard against someone or something. ---
examples: Crews battle wildfires along the coast every August.
He battled the insurance company for eighteen months.
She has been battling a cold all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she battled cancer for years), intransitive (the two sides battled over the bill)

entries.meaning: To cry or shout very loudly. ---
examples: Babies bawl when they are hungry.
She bawled through the whole ceremony.
He was bawling into the phone by the time I got there.
entries.contrast: bawl sounds exactly like ball.

entries.meaning: To pull a boat up onto the shore, or of a sea animal, to become stranded on land. ---
examples: We usually beach the kayaks near the point.
A young whale beached south of the pier on Tuesday.
The ferry has been beached since the storm.
entries.русский: вытаскивать на берег; выбрасываться на берег
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (beach the canoe above the tide line), intransitive (three whales beached overnight)
entries.contrast: Ends in -ch, so the third person adds -es: beaches. It sounds like beech, the tree.

entries.meaning: To smile broadly with happiness, or to send out light or a signal. ---
examples: The satellites beam the game to half the world.
She beamed when they called her name.
He was beaming all the way through the ceremony.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they beamed the signal to the station), intransitive (she beamed at the news)

entries.meaning: To make a place or a thing look more attractive. ---
examples: Volunteers beautify the park every spring.
The city beautified the waterfront ahead of the festival.
They have been beautifying the old train station for months.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie-: beautifies, beautified, but the -ing form keeps it: beautifying.

entries.meaning: To be suitable or proper for someone or something. ---
examples: Wear something that will befit a formal dinner.
The town gave the old teacher a send-off that befitted forty years of service.
She accepted the prize with a modesty befitting her age.
entries.contrast: The final t doubles: befit - befitted - befitting.

entries.meaning: To confuse someone so badly that they cannot think clearly. ---
examples: Long legal sentences befuddle most readers.
The magician befuddled the audience with one simple card.
He looked completely befuddled when I mentioned the deadline.

entries.meaning: To feel resentment about what someone has or about giving something up. ---
examples: I don't begrudge her the promotion; she earned it.
Nobody begrudged him a day off after that week.
She has never begrudged a dollar spent on her children's schooling.
entries.contrast: Takes two objects: begrudge SOMEONE SOMETHING (begrudge him his success).

entries.meaning: To charm someone, often in a way that misleads them. ---
examples: Street performers beguile the crowd with impossible tricks.
The salesman beguiled them into signing a terrible lease.
It is a beguiling idea, but the numbers do not work.

entries.meaning: To cut off someone's head. ---
examples: In the play the queen threatens to behead anyone who lies to her.
Anne Boleyn was beheaded in 1536.
Two of the marble figures had been beheaded long before the museum bought them.

entries.meaning: To be necessary or sensible for someone to do something. ---
examples: It would behoove you to read the contract before you sign it.
It behooved the company to settle the case quickly.
It behooves every driver to check the tires before a long trip.
entries.contrast: American behoove, British behove. Almost always used with it: it behooves someone TO do something.

entries.meaning: To decorate something with jewels. ---
examples: The designers bejewel every gown by hand.
She bejeweled the costume with hundreds of tiny stones.
A bejeweled crown sat alone in the glass case.
entries.contrast: American keeps one l: bejeweled, bejeweling. British doubles it: bejewelled, bejewelling.

entries.meaning: To keep going over something long after the point has been made. ---
examples: I don't want to belabor the point, but we are out of time.
The speaker belabored the same statistic for ten minutes.
He has a habit of belaboring details everyone already understands.
entries.contrast: American belabor, British belabour.

entries.meaning: To let gas out of the stomach noisily through the mouth, or to send something out in thick clouds. ---
examples: Please don't belch at the table.
The old bus belched black smoke as it pulled away.
Factory chimneys were belching steam into the cold morning air.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the engine belched smoke), intransitive (he belched loudly)

entries.meaning: To surround someone with troubles or with an army so that there is no easy escape. ---
examples: Lawsuits beleaguer the company on every side.
Bad weather beleaguered the expedition for a week.
The beleaguered mayor resigned on Friday.

entries.meaning: To give a false impression of something, or to show that something is not true. ---
examples: A cheerful tone can belie real anxiety.
The calm surface belied the current running underneath.
His boyish face has always belied his age.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e and keep the y: belies, belied, belying. Not the same as lie (to lie down, to tell a lie).

entries.meaning: To shout or roar in a deep, very loud voice. ---
examples: Coaches bellow instructions from the sideline all game.
The sergeant bellowed an order across the yard.
We could hear him bellowing at the umpire from the top row.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he bellowed an order), intransitive (she bellowed at the referee)
entries.contrast: Not the word below: bellow is BEL-oh with stress on the first syllable, below is bi-LOH.

entries.meaning: To complain on and on in a whiny, annoying way. ---
examples: They bellyache about the coffee every single morning.
He bellyached for an hour about the new parking rules.
Stop bellyaching and finish the job.
entries.contrast: Informal. Complain bellyache ABOUT something. The -y stays because belly joins ache as one word.

entries.meaning: To hit something or someone hard with a swinging blow. ---
examples: Don't belt your brother over a video game.
She belted the ball over the left-field fence.
He has belted thirty home runs this season.

entries.meaning: To complain about something or express sorrow over it. ---
examples: Critics bemoan the loss of small bookstores.
She bemoaned the state of the roads the whole drive home.
Owners are bemoaning another rise in rent.

entries.meaning: To puzzle or bewilder someone. ---
examples: The question seemed to bemuse the witness.
His answer bemused the entire committee.
She watched the argument with a bemused smile.
entries.contrast: Not amuse. Bemused means puzzled, not entertained.

entries.meaning: To measure something against a standard or against what rivals achieve. ---
examples: We benchmark our prices against the two largest chains.
The lab benchmarked the new chip at twice the old speed.
They are benchmarking salaries across the whole industry.
entries.contrast: Benchmark something AGAINST something else.

entries.meaning: To damage someone's reputation or good name. ---
examples: He said the rumors were meant to besmirch his record.
One scandal besmirched a family name that had stood for a century.
She sued the paper for besmirching her reputation.

entries.meaning: To defeat someone in a contest or an argument. ---
examples: Very few players can best her at chess.
The underdog bested the champion in three straight sets.
He has been bested only twice all season.
entries.contrast: As a verb, best means to beat someone, not to do your best.

entries.meaning: To improve something, or to do better than an earlier result. ---
examples: He took night classes to better his chances of promotion.
She bettered the school record by two full seconds.
The program helps families who are bettering their standard of living.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double again: bettered, bettering.

entries.meaning: To cut a sloping edge on a piece of wood, glass, or metal. ---
examples: We bevel the edges so that nobody cuts a finger.
The carpenter beveled the edge of the mirror.
A beveled glass panel catches the light beautifully.
entries.contrast: American keeps one l: beveled, beveling. British doubles it: bevelled, bevelling.

entries.meaning: To put a spell on someone, or to charm someone completely. ---
examples: The old stories say that a single glance can bewitch a traveler.
Her voice bewitched the whole audience.
He stood at the window, bewitched by the view.

entries.meaning: To influence someone or something unfairly in one direction. ---
examples: A loaded question can bias an entire survey.
Early news reports biased the jury against him.
The sample is biased toward younger users.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one s: biased, biasing. Bias someone AGAINST or TOWARD something.

entries.meaning: To travel somewhere by bicycle. ---
examples: They bicycle to work in almost any weather.
We bicycled along the coast for three days.
She spent the summer bicycling through Vermont.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: bicycling, not bicycleing.

entries.meaning: To divide into two branches or parts. ---
examples: Streams like this often bifurcate before they reach the sea.
The judge bifurcated the trial into a guilt phase and a damages phase.
The company has bifurcated into two separate businesses.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the judge bifurcated the trial), intransitive (the trail bifurcates)

entries.meaning: To cheat someone out of money. ---
examples: Scammers bilk older people out of their savings every year.
He bilked investors out of two million dollars.
She was charged with bilking the charity she ran.
entries.contrast: Usually bilk someone OUT OF money.

entries.meaning: To do something to excess in a short burst, especially eating, drinking, or watching episodes. ---
examples: They binge on snacks every time exams come around.
We binged the entire season in one weekend.
He has been bingeing on old detective shows all month.
entries.русский: предаваться излишествам; смотреть или есть запоем
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (we binged the whole season), intransitive (he binged on chocolate)
entries.contrast: The -ing form usually keeps the e: bingeing (binging is also seen). Binge ON food or drink.

entries.meaning: To break down naturally through the action of bacteria and other living things. ---
examples: These cups biodegrade in about ninety days.
The test bags biodegraded completely within a year.
Ocean plastic is still not biodegrading the way the label promised.

entries.meaning: To divide something into two equal parts. ---
examples: Use a compass to bisect the angle exactly.
A new highway bisected the old neighborhood.
The park is bisected by a narrow stream.

entries.meaning: To camp for the night outdoors with little or no shelter. ---
examples: Climbers often bivouac on the ledge below the summit.
The troops bivouacked in a field outside the town.
We spent that night bivouacking under an overhang.
entries.русский: располагаться биваком, ночевать под открытым небом
entries.contrast: A k appears before the ending: bivouacked, bivouacking. Same rule as panic - panicked.

entries.meaning: To vote against letting someone join a group, or to shut someone out of a profession. ---
examples: A single member can blackball a candidate.
The studio blackballed him after the lawsuit.
He claims he has been blackballed by every agency in town.

entries.meaning: To make something black or dark, or to become black or dark. ---
examples: Smoke from the stove will blacken the ceiling over time.
Storm clouds blackened the sky before noon.
The beams had been blackened by years of soot.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (smoke blackened the walls), intransitive (the sky blackened)

entries.meaning: To put someone or something on a list of those to be refused or avoided. ---
examples: Most mail servers blacklist addresses that send spam.
The airline blacklisted the passenger after the incident.
Several screenwriters were blacklisted during the 1950s.

entries.meaning: To speak about God or sacred things with disrespect. ---
examples: In several countries it is still a crime to blaspheme.
He was accused of having blasphemed in the article.
The crowd shouted that the preacher was blaspheming.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he blasphemed the name of God), intransitive (they accused her of blaspheming)
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (blas-FEEM); the noun blasphemy is stressed on the first (BLAS-fuh-mee).

entries.meaning: To make the thin, shaky cry of a sheep or goat, or to complain in a weak, whiny voice. ---
examples: The goats bleat whenever anyone walks past the fence.
A lamb bleated somewhere behind the barn.
He kept bleating about how unfair the schedule was.

entries.meaning: To make a person or a system seriously weak. ---
examples: Long hospital stays debilitate even young patients.
The infection debilitated him for months.
She was debilitated by the treatment, not by the disease itself.

entries.meaning: To take money out of a bank account. ---
examples: The gym will debit your account on the first of every month.
They debited the full amount twice by mistake.
The fee has already been debited.
entries.contrast: One t: debited, debiting — the stress is on DEB-. The opposite of credit.

entries.meaning: To take the bones out of meat or fish before cooking. ---
examples: Ask the butcher to debone the chicken thighs.
He deboned the trout in about a minute.
The fillets come already deboned.

entries.meaning: To show that a popular belief or claim is false. ---
examples: Nutritionists debunk this diet myth every January.
The reporter debunked the story in one afternoon.
That theory has been debunked many times over.

entries.meaning: To remove most of the caffeine from coffee or tea. ---
examples: They decaffeinate the beans with water instead of chemicals.
The company decaffeinated its whole house blend.
I only drink decaffeinated coffee after six.

entries.meaning: To leave a place suddenly, usually for somewhere better. ---
examples: Every August half the office decamps to the coast.
The band decamped to Nashville to record.
Fans were already decamping to the parking lot in the eighth inning.
entries.русский: внезапно уезжать, перебираться; сниматься с места
entries.contrast: You decamp to or for a new place.

entries.meaning: To pour liquid slowly from one container into another, leaving the sediment behind. ---
examples: Let the wine breathe, or decant it into a pitcher.
She decanted the soup into three jars.
The oil is decanted into smaller bottles for the table.

entries.meaning: To cut off the head of a person or an animal. ---
examples: Vandals decapitate the garden statues almost every spring.
The hailstorm decapitated every sunflower in the row.
The bronze figure had been decapitated sometime in the 1800s.

entries.meaning: To cut the carbon emissions of an industry, a building, or a country to nearly zero. ---
examples: The plan is to decarbonize the power grid by 2035.
Steelmakers decarbonized faster than anyone expected.
Shipping is decarbonizing more slowly than aviation.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decarbonize the grid), intransitive (heavy industry must decarbonize)
entries.contrast: American decarbonize; British writing uses decarbonise.

entries.meaning: To slow down, or to make something slow down. ---
examples: Loaded trucks decelerate slowly on wet pavement.
Inflation decelerated for the fourth month in a row.
The train was decelerating as it entered the tunnel.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decelerate the car), intransitive (growth decelerated)
entries.contrast: The opposite of accelerate.

entries.meaning: To move power or operations away from one central place to many smaller ones. ---
examples: The reform would decentralize hiring to individual schools.
The company decentralized its support teams last year.
Health care has been steadily decentralized since the 1990s.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decentralize the agency), intransitive (the network decentralized)
entries.contrast: American decentralize; British decentralise.

entries.meaning: To officially take away a license, an accreditation, or a union's recognition. ---
examples: The state can decertify an officer who lies under oath.
Regulators decertified two nursing homes in the county.
The union was decertified after a very close vote.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: decertifies, decertified, but decertifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To destroy a large part of a group or a population. ---
examples: Two bad winters can decimate a bee colony.
The layoffs decimated the newsroom.
Whole villages had been decimated by the epidemic.

entries.meaning: To knock someone to the ground with a punch. ---
examples: One more word and I'll deck him.
He decked the guy in front of the whole bar.
The catcher got decked at home plate.
entries.contrast: Informal. Not the same as the phrasal deck out, which means to decorate.

entries.meaning: To remove the secret status from official documents so that the public can read them. ---
examples: Agencies declassify thousands of pages every year.
The White House declassified the memo on a Friday.
The cables were declassified thirty years later.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: declassifies, declassified, but declassifying.

entries.meaning: To remove an animal's claws, or to take the force out of something. ---
examples: Most American vets now refuse to declaw cats.
Amendments declawed the bill before the final vote.
The agency has been declawed by three rounds of budget cuts.

entries.meaning: To free a country from colonial rule, or to strip colonial assumptions out of a subject. ---
examples: Britain began to decolonize Africa after the war.
Ghana was decolonized in 1957.
Several universities are decolonizing their reading lists.

entries.meaning: To take a ship, a power plant, or a piece of equipment permanently out of service. ---
examples: The Navy will decommission the carrier next spring.
They decommissioned the reactor in 2019.
The rig has been decommissioned and towed away.

entries.meaning: To open up a compressed file, or to unwind after a stressful stretch. ---
examples: The app will decompress the archive automatically.
I decompressed for a week after the trial ended.
He's still decompressing from the move.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decompress the file), intransitive (I need to decompress)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ss: decompresses.

entries.meaning: To break an idea, a text, or a dish down into its parts in order to examine them. ---
examples: Critics love to deconstruct his early films.
The coach deconstructed every play on video.
The menu features a deconstructed apple pie.

entries.meaning: To remove dangerous chemicals, radiation, or germs from a place or a person. ---
examples: Crews decontaminate the suits after every shift.
They decontaminated the soil around the old plant.
The whole ward had to be decontaminated.

entries.meaning: To separate two things that used to move or work together. ---
examples: The proposal would decouple health insurance from employment.
The two markets decoupled for most of the year.
Emissions are slowly decoupling from economic growth.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decouple pay from hours), intransitive (the two markets decoupled)
entries.contrast: You decouple one thing from another.

entries.meaning: To order something officially, by the authority of a ruler or a court. ---
examples: A president cannot simply decree a new tax.
The king decreed a day of mourning.
The judge has decreed that the records stay sealed.
entries.contrast: Both e's stay: decreed, decreeing. Compare agree — agreed — agreeing.

entries.meaning: To change the law so that something is no longer a crime. ---
examples: Several states have voted to decriminalize small amounts.
Portugal decriminalized drug possession in 2001.
Jaywalking has been decriminalized in California.
entries.contrast: American decriminalize; British decriminalise.

entries.meaning: To condemn something publicly and strongly. ---
examples: Editorials decry the ruling almost daily.
Both parties decried the violence.
The mayor has been decrying the cuts all week.
entries.contrast: The -y follows a consonant: decries, decried, but decrying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To transfer property to someone by a legal document. ---
examples: Her parents plan to deed the farm to the county.
He deeded the house to his daughter in 1998.
The land was deeded to the city for a park.
entries.русский: передавать по дарственной, оформлять передачу собственности
entries.contrast: You deed property to someone.

entries.meaning: To make a conflict or a tense situation calmer and less dangerous. ---
examples: Officers are trained to deescalate before they draw a weapon.
The talks deescalated the crisis for a few months.
Tensions have been deescalating since the ceasefire.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (deescalate the situation), intransitive (the standoff deescalated)
entries.contrast: Usually written with a hyphen: de-escalate, de-escalated. The opposite of escalate.

entries.meaning: To damage someone's reputation by saying or printing untrue things about them. ---
examples: You cannot defame a public figure without proving malice.
The paper defamed him and paid for it in court.
She claims she was defamed on the podcast.

entries.meaning: To take away something's power to do harm. ---
examples: Lobbyists worked all spring to defang the regulation.
One amendment defanged the whole bill.
The committee has been defanged by the new rules.

entries.meaning: To fail to pay back a loan, or to fall back automatically on a standard option. ---
examples: If the country defaults, borrowing gets much more expensive.
He defaulted on two student loans.
The form kept defaulting to last year's address.
entries.русский: не выполнять обязательства, объявлять дефолт; выбираться по умолчанию
entries.contrast: You default on a loan; a setting defaults to a value.

entries.meaning: To pass solid waste out of the body. ---
examples: Most newborns defecate several times a day.
The dog defecated on the neighbor's lawn.
A patient who has not defecated in three days should call the office.
entries.contrast: The clinical word. In conversation Americans say poop or go to the bathroom.

entries.meaning: To spoil something clean or sacred by treating it with disrespect. ---
examples: Runoff from the mine defiles the creek every spring.
Someone defiled the memorial with spray paint.
The temple had been defiled and then abandoned.

entries.meaning: To let the air out of something, or to make someone lose their confidence. ---
examples: Deflate the raft before you roll it up.
One comment from her deflated him completely.
The balloon was deflating faster than we could patch it.
entries.русский: сдувать, спускать воздух; сдуваться; сбивать спесь
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (deflate the tire), intransitive (the raft deflated)

entries.meaning: To strip the leaves off trees and plants, usually with chemicals or insects. ---
examples: Gypsy moths can defoliate an entire hillside.
The military defoliated thousands of square miles of jungle.
The orchard was almost completely defoliated by June.

entries.meaning: To cut down all the trees over a large area. ---
examples: Cattle ranching deforests more land than logging does.
Settlers deforested the valley within a generation.
Much of the basin has already been deforested.

entries.meaning: To change the shape of something so that it is bent or spoiled. ---
examples: Heat will deform the plastic housing.
The impact deformed the front wheel.
The beams were deforming under the weight of the snow.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heat deforms the plastic), intransitive (the frame deformed)

entries.meaning: To pay part or all of someone's costs. ---
examples: The grant helps defray travel expenses.
A bake sale defrayed most of the cost of the trip.
Tuition is partly defrayed by the scholarship.
entries.contrast: The -y follows a vowel, so it stays: defrays, defrayed. Compare carry — carried.

entries.meaning: To remove a priest or minister from the clergy as a punishment. ---
examples: The church can defrock a priest without a criminal trial.
The diocese defrocked him in 2004.
Two defrocked priests testified at the hearing.

entries.meaning: To stop providing money to an organization or a program. ---
examples: Congress threatened to defund the agency.
The state defunded the program in 2011.
Arts education has been quietly defunded for years.

entries.meaning: To get steadily worse, or to sink into a lower and uglier state. ---
examples: These meetings always degenerate into shouting.
The debate degenerated within ten minutes.
His eyesight has been degenerating since the surgery.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in -rayt; the adjective and noun end in a schwa: dih-JEN-uh-ruht. Usually degenerate into something.

entries.meaning: To pour liquid into a hot pan to loosen the browned bits and make a sauce. ---
examples: Deglaze the pan with a splash of white wine.
She deglazed the skillet with stock and poured it over the meat.
Deglazing takes about thirty seconds.
entries.contrast: You deglaze a pan with wine, stock, or water.

entries.meaning: To treat or portray people as though they were not human beings. ---
examples: Propaganda works by dehumanizing the other side.
The system dehumanized everyone who passed through it.
Prisoners described being dehumanized by the daily routine.
entries.contrast: American dehumanize; British dehumanise.

entries.meaning: To remove moisture from the air in a room or a building. ---
examples: A small unit will dehumidify the whole basement.
We dehumidified the crawl space before laying the floor.
The machine has been dehumidifying for two days.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: dehumidifies, dehumidified, but dehumidifying.

entries.meaning: To remove ice from a surface, especially an aircraft or a windshield. ---
examples: Crews deice the wings right before takeoff.
They deiced the plane twice and we still missed our slot.
The runway is being deiced now.
entries.русский: очищать ото льда, обрабатывать противообледенительным составом
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen: de-ice, de-iced, de-icing.

entries.meaning: To treat a person or a thing as if it were a god. ---
examples: Fans deify a coach after one good season.
Rome deified several of its emperors.
He has been deified by an industry that once ignored him.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: deifies, deified, but deifying.

entries.meaning: To do something you consider beneath you, as though it were a favor. ---
examples: He won't even deign to answer the email.
She finally deigned to look up from her phone.
They have never deigned to explain the decision.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: DAYN, like Dane. Almost always deign to do something.

entries.meaning: To make an institution, a leader, or a result seem not legitimate. ---
examples: Endless lawsuits delegitimize the whole process.
The broadcast delegitimized the election in the eyes of millions.
The court has been delegitimized by the fight over appointments.

entries.meaning: To describe or mark out something clearly and in detail. ---
examples: The contract should delineate each party's duties.
The treaty delineated the border river by river.
Responsibilities are carefully delineated in the handbook.

entries.meaning: To remove a company from a stock exchange, or an item from an official list. ---
examples: The exchange can delist a stock that trades under a dollar.
Nasdaq delisted the company in March.
The species was delisted once the population recovered.
entries.русский: исключать из списка, снимать с биржевых торгов

entries.meaning: To make someone believe something that is not true. ---
examples: Don't delude yourself about the numbers.
He deluded investors for six years.
They were deluded into thinking the job was safe.
entries.contrast: Very often reflexive: delude yourself.

entries.meaning: To take the magnetism out of something. ---
examples: A phone case can demagnetize a hotel key.
The scanner demagnetized my credit card.
The strip has been demagnetized, so you'll need a new card.

entries.meaning: To mark or fix the boundary between two things or areas. ---
examples: Orange cones demarcate the work zone.
The treaty demarcated the two territories in 1904.
The two roles are not clearly demarcated.

entries.meaning: To remove armed forces and weapons from an area. ---
examples: Both sides agreed to demilitarize the border.
The islands were demilitarized after the war.
They are demilitarizing the zone one checkpoint at a time.
entries.contrast: American demilitarize; British demilitarise.

entries.meaning: To show how a product works by using it in front of people. ---
examples: She'll demo the new release at the conference.
They demoed the app for us over lunch.
We've been demoing the machine in stores all month.
entries.contrast: The o stays in every form: demos, demoed, demoing.

entries.meaning: To send soldiers home and take an army out of active service. ---
examples: The agreement requires both armies to demobilize.
Washington demobilized millions of men in 1945.
Fighters are being demobilized under UN supervision.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (demobilize the troops), intransitive (the militia demobilized)

entries.meaning: To give far more people access to something, or to make a country democratic. ---
examples: Cheap cameras democratize filmmaking.
The reforms democratized the party's nominating process.
Access to data has been democratized by these tools.
entries.contrast: American democratize; British democratise.

entries.meaning: To stop a video or a channel from earning money, or to take a banknote out of circulation. ---
examples: Platforms demonetize videos that mention certain topics.
India demonetized its two largest banknotes in 2016.
Her whole channel was demonetized overnight.
entries.русский: демонетизировать, лишать возможности зарабатывать; изымать из обращения

entries.meaning: To portray a person or a group as evil. ---
examples: Campaigns demonize whoever is easiest to blame.
The coverage demonized an entire neighborhood.
Immigrants have been demonized in every recession.
entries.contrast: American demonize; British demonise.

entries.meaning: To take away someone's confidence, hope, or willingness to keep going. ---
examples: Long shifts and no raise demoralize even good nurses.
The loss demoralized the whole team.
The staff is completely demoralized.
entries.contrast: American demoralize; British demoralise.

entries.meaning: To move someone to a lower rank or position. ---
examples: They may demote him rather than fire him.
The league demoted two officials after the review.
He was demoted to a desk job in March.
entries.contrast: The opposite of promote.

entries.meaning: To make someone lose interest in working or trying. ---
examples: Nothing demotivates a team faster than a pointless meeting.
The new quota demotivated half the sales floor.
Students are demotivated by grading they don't understand.

entries.meaning: To object politely, or to hesitate rather than agree. ---
examples: Two board members demur whenever the topic comes up.
She demurred when reporters asked about the money.
He was still demurring an hour into the negotiation.
entries.русский: возражать, выражать несогласие; уклоняться от ответа
entries.contrast: The r doubles: demurred, demurring. Not the adjective demure (dih-MYOOR, 'modest and quiet').

entries.meaning: To make a difficult or mysterious subject easy to understand. ---
examples: The book tries to demystify the tax code.
Her lecture demystified the whole process.
He spends his weekends demystifying statistics for beginners.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: demystifies, demystified, but demystifying.

entries.meaning: To change the natural structure of a protein, or to make alcohol unfit to drink. ---
examples: Heat and acid both denature egg proteins.
The sample denatured at seventy degrees.
Industrial alcohol is denatured so that nobody will drink it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heat denatures the protein), intransitive (the enzyme denatured)

entries.meaning: To criticize someone or something unfairly in order to make them seem worthless. ---
examples: He never denigrates his competitors in public.
The review denigrated the entire genre.
Her work was denigrated for years before anyone reconsidered it.

entries.meaning: To be a sign of something, or to stand for it. ---
examples: In this table an asterisk denotes an estimate.
The red line denoted the old border.
The suffix has always denoted something small.
entries.contrast: Denote is what a word or sign literally stands for; connote is what it suggests.

entries.meaning: To strip a place bare of its covering, especially of plants or soil. ---
examples: Overgrazing can denude a hillside in a single season.
Logging denuded the ridge above the town.
The slopes had been denuded long before the flood.

entries.meaning: To be decided by something else, or to rely on someone for support. ---
examples: How long it takes depends on the weather.
The whole town depended on one factory.
Thousands of families are depending on that check.
entries.contrast: Always depend on (or upon) something — never 'depend of'.

entries.meaning: To get off an airplane. ---
examples: Passengers in rows twenty and up may deplane now.
We deplaned on the tarmac in the rain.
They were still deplaning when our flight started boarding.
entries.contrast: Airline English. In conversation Americans say get off the plane.

entries.meaning: To say strongly and publicly that you think something is very wrong. ---
examples: We deplore the use of force against protesters.
The statement deplored the attack but named no one.
Such language has been deplored by every previous chair.

entries.meaning: To greatly reduce the number of people living in a place. ---
examples: Factory closures can depopulate a small town in a decade.
War and famine depopulated the province.
Whole counties have been depopulated since the 1980s.

entries.meaning: To remove a ruler from power, or to question a witness under oath before a trial. ---
examples: Generals rarely depose a leader without foreign help.
The army deposed the president in 1973.
Both executives have already been deposed by the plaintiffs' lawyers.
entries.русский: свергать, смещать; снимать показания под присягой

entries.meaning: To express disapproval of something, or to mark a software feature as outdated. ---
examples: Most style guides deprecate this construction.
The team deprecated the old API last spring.
That function has been deprecated — use the new one.
entries.русский: не одобрять, осуждать; объявлять устаревшим (в IT)
entries.contrast: Not depreciate, which is about losing value. Note self-deprecating, 'making fun of oneself'.

entries.meaning: To fall in value over time, or to write down the value of an asset. ---
examples: A new car starts to depreciate the moment you drive it off the lot.
The peso depreciated sharply against the dollar.
The equipment is being depreciated over five years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (depreciate the equipment), intransitive (a new car depreciates)
entries.contrast: Depreciate is about value; deprecate is about disapproval.

entries.meaning: To release the pressure inside a sealed container or an aircraft cabin. ---
examples: Technicians depressurize the tank before opening it.
The cabin depressurized at thirty thousand feet.
The chamber is slowly depressurizing.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (depressurize the tank), intransitive (the cabin depressurized)

entries.meaning: To treat something as less important than it was before. ---
examples: Let's deprioritize the redesign until after launch.
Management deprioritized the whole feature.
Maintenance has been deprioritized for three budget cycles.

entries.meaning: To free someone from beliefs that a cult or a movement pushed on them. ---
examples: Families sometimes hire specialists to deprogram a relative.
It took two years to deprogram him.
She writes about being deprogrammed in the 1980s.
entries.contrast: The m doubles: deprogrammed, deprogramming — like program — programmed.

entries.meaning: To give someone official power to act for you, especially as a deputy. ---
examples: A sheriff can deputize ordinary citizens in an emergency.
He deputized two ranchers to help with the search.
The volunteers were deputized that same afternoon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the sheriff deputized them), intransitive (he deputized for the chair)
entries.contrast: American deputize; British deputise.

entries.meaning: To remove government rules from an industry. ---
examples: Both parties promised to deregulate small banks.
Congress deregulated the airlines in 1978.
Trucking has been deregulated for decades.

entries.meaning: To speak about someone or something with open contempt. ---
examples: Critics deride the plan as a giveaway.
Reviewers derided the film when it came out.
The idea was derided for years and then quietly adopted.
entries.contrast: Often deride something as something: derided it as a stunt.

entries.meaning: To remove the salt from seawater so that it can be used or drunk. ---
examples: The plant can desalinate fifty million gallons a day.
Israel desalinated its way out of a water crisis.
Most of the city's water is now desalinated.

entries.meaning: To damage or show great disrespect for a holy or honored place. ---
examples: It is a felony to desecrate a grave.
Someone desecrated the synagogue over the weekend.
The chapel had been desecrated during the occupation.

entries.meaning: To end the legal separation of racial groups in schools or public places. ---
examples: The ruling ordered the district to desegregate.
Little Rock desegregated Central High in 1957.
Many school systems were never fully desegregated.

entries.meaning: To remove something from a set of selected items, usually by clicking it again. ---
examples: Deselect every box except the first one.
I deselected the photos I didn't want.
Nothing happens until all the layers are deselected.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something less sensitive or less easily affected. ---
examples: Violent images can desensitize young viewers.
Years of coverage desensitized the public.
Patients are gradually desensitized to the allergen.
entries.contrast: American desensitize; British desensitise. You desensitize someone to something.

entries.meaning: To dry something out completely. ---
examples: A hot wind can desiccate a field in two days.
The drought desiccated the whole valley.
The recipe calls for desiccated coconut.
entries.contrast: One s, then double c: desiccate, desiccated.

entries.meaning: To officially choose something for a purpose, or to give it a name or a status. ---
examples: The city will designate two blocks as a historic district.
Congress designated the area a national monument in 1996.
He has been designated as the acting director.
entries.contrast: Here the g is pronounced: DEZ-ig-nayt — unlike design, dih-ZYN.

entries.meaning: To want something strongly. ---
examples: Most parents desire a better life for their children.
She had long desired a place of her own.
He got everything he had ever desired and still felt empty.

entries.meaning: To rob a place of its beauty or its valuable things. ---
examples: Cheap development can despoil an entire coastline.
The invaders despoiled every village along the river.
The valley has been despoiled by decades of strip mining.

entries.meaning: To make a country, a system or a situation less steady and more likely to fail. ---
examples: A rumor like that can destabilize the whole market.
The coup destabilized the region for a decade.
The currency has been destabilized by months of protest.
entries.contrast: American destabilize; British destabilise.

entries.meaning: To make people stop treating something as shameful. ---
examples: The campaign is trying to destigmatize asking for help.
That one film destigmatized therapy for a lot of viewers.
Mental illness is slowly being destigmatized in the workplace.

entries.meaning: To set someone or something aside in advance for a particular purpose or fate. ---
examples: Nothing in his childhood seemed to destine him for politics.
Her parents destined her for medicine before she could walk.
The plan was destined to fail from the very first meeting.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive: be destined for something, be destined to do something.

entries.meaning: To separate hair, cords or threads that have become knotted together. ---
examples: This spray helps detangle wet hair.
She detangled the headphone cords before packing them.
We spent an hour detangling the Christmas lights.

entries.meaning: To clear alcohol, drugs or other harmful substances out of the body. ---
examples: He checked into a clinic to detox.
She detoxed for a week before the surgery.
After three days of detoxing, he finally slept through the night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (detox the body), intransitive (he detoxed in a clinic)

entries.meaning: To remove poisonous substances from a body, a substance or a place. ---
examples: The liver detoxifies the blood around the clock.
Crews detoxified the soil before the park was built.
The patient had to be detoxified over two days.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: detoxifies, detoxified, but detoxifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To make something seem less good or less valuable. ---
examples: One weak chapter does not detract from the book.
The noise detracted from an otherwise perfect evening.
Nothing has detracted from her reputation as a teacher.
entries.contrast: Almost always with from: detract from the value, never 'detract the value'.

entries.meaning: To reduce the worth of money, work or a person's contribution. ---
examples: Printing money like that can devalue the currency overnight.
The government devalued the peso in August.
Teachers say they feel devalued by the new rules.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (devalue the currency), intransitive (the peso devalued sharply)

entries.meaning: To move away from an expected course, plan or standard. ---
examples: Don't deviate from the recipe the first time you make it.
The plane deviated from its route to avoid the storm.
He has never deviated from that position in public.
entries.contrast: Takes from: deviate from the plan.

entries.meaning: To pass power or duties down to a lower level, or to sink into a worse state. ---
examples: Arguments like that usually devolve into name-calling.
The debate quickly devolved into a shouting match.
Most of these decisions have been devolved to the states.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (devolve power to the regions), intransitive (the talks devolved into shouting)
entries.contrast: Devolve into means to deteriorate into; devolve to means to be handed down to.

entries.meaning: To stop living. ---
examples: Plants die quickly without water.
His grandfather died last spring.
The battery is dying and the screen keeps going black.
entries.contrast: The -ing form drops ie for y: dying, never 'dieing'. Do not confuse it with dye — dyed — dyeing, which means to color cloth.

entries.meaning: To be unlike something else, or to hold a different opinion. ---
examples: The two reports differ on almost every number.
Their accounts differed in one crucial detail.
Historians have differed about the cause for a century.
entries.contrast: Differ from means to be unlike; differ with means to disagree with. The stress is on the first syllable, so the r does not double: differed, differing.

entries.meaning: To spread something out over a wide area, or to spread out in that way. ---
examples: Thin curtains diffuse the afternoon light nicely.
The smell of coffee diffused through the whole apartment.
The heat is diffused evenly by the metal plate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (diffuse the light), intransitive (the smell diffused through the room)
entries.contrast: Not defuse (dee-FYOOZ), which means to make a bomb or a tense situation safe. The adjective diffuse ends in an s sound: dih-FYOOS.

entries.meaning: To treat something as worthy of serious attention or respect. ---
examples: I won't dignify that question with an answer.
He dignified the small ceremony simply by showing up.
The rumors have never been dignified with a response.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: dignifies, dignified, but dignifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To wander away from the main subject while speaking or writing. ---
examples: But I digress — back to the main point.
The lecturer digressed for ten minutes about his cat.
He kept digressing until we ran out of time.

entries.meaning: To make an opening in the body wider, or to become wider. ---
examples: Your pupils dilate in the dark.
The doctor dilated her eyes before the exam.
He arrived with his pupils still dilated from the drops.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the drops dilate the pupils), intransitive (her pupils dilated)

entries.meaning: To make something dirty. ---
examples: Take your shoes off so you don't dirty the rug.
The kids dirtied every towel in the house.
Her white coat was dirtied by spray from the road.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie before -s and -d: dirties, dirtied, but dirtying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To free someone of a belief that is not true. ---
examples: Let me disabuse you of that idea right now.
One week on the job disabused her of any romantic notions about it.
He has been disabused of the belief that hard work is always enough.
entries.contrast: Takes of: disabuse someone of an idea.

entries.meaning: To stop being visible, or to stop existing. ---
examples: Socks disappear in this building's laundry room.
The sun disappeared behind the clouds.
Two hikers have disappeared in the park this month.
entries.contrast: Spelling trap: one s but two p's — disappear, disappeared.

entries.meaning: To think that something is bad or wrong. ---
examples: My parents disapprove of the whole plan.
The committee disapproved the request without a hearing.
She has always disapproved of gossip.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the board disapproved the request), intransitive (my parents disapprove of him)
entries.contrast: In the everyday sense it takes of: disapprove of smoking.

entries.meaning: To take a machine or a structure apart into its separate pieces. ---
examples: You have to disassemble the bed to get it through the door.
He disassembled the engine on the kitchen table.
The stage was disassembled in under an hour.
entries.contrast: Not dissemble, which means to hide your real feelings.

entries.meaning: To say publicly that you have no connection with something or no longer support it. ---
examples: The senator was quick to disavow the ad.
The group disavowed any link to the attack.
He has publicly disavowed everything he wrote back then.

entries.meaning: To take away a lawyer's right to practice law. ---
examples: The state can disbar an attorney for stealing from clients.
The court disbarred him two years ago.
She was disbarred after the fraud came to light.
entries.русский: лишать адвокатского статуса, лишить права практики
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: disbarred, disbarring.

entries.meaning: To refuse to accept that something is true. ---
examples: I have no reason to disbelieve her.
The jury clearly disbelieved the witness.
His account was disbelieved by everyone in the room.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the jury disbelieved him), intransitive (she had no reason to disbelieve)

entries.meaning: To pay out money from a fund that has been set aside. ---
examples: The foundation will disburse the grants in May.
The agency disbursed four million dollars last year.
Aid has already been disbursed to three provinces.
entries.contrast: Not disperse (to scatter). Disburse is about paying money out.

entries.meaning: To state officially that you have no responsibility for something or no claim to it. ---
examples: The site disclaims any responsibility for what users post.
The company disclaimed all knowledge of the leak.
He has disclaimed his share of the inheritance in writing.

entries.meaning: To change the color of something for the worse, usually by staining or fading. ---
examples: Coffee will discolor your teeth over time.
The sun discolored the curtains in a single summer.
The wall was discolored where the water got in.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (coffee discolors teeth), intransitive (the pages discolored with age)
entries.contrast: American discolor, discolored; British discolour, discoloured.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel uneasy or unsure of themselves. ---
examples: A silence like that can disconcert even a good speaker.
His steady stare disconcerted her.
The audience was disconcerted by the sudden blackout.

entries.meaning: To make people stop believing or respecting someone or something. ---
examples: The defense tried to discredit the witness.
New data discredited the original study.
The theory has been thoroughly discredited.

entries.meaning: To get off a ship, a plane or a train. ---
examples: Passengers disembark through the rear door.
We disembarked in Naples at dawn.
The troops had already disembarked by midnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they disembarked the passengers first), intransitive (we disembarked at noon)

entries.meaning: To make someone stop believing that something is as good as they thought. ---
examples: A year in the industry can disenchant almost anyone.
The scandal disenchanted many longtime fans.
Voters have grown disenchanted with both parties.
entries.contrast: Usually passive, with with: disenchanted with politics.

entries.meaning: To free something from knots, or to separate things that have become confused with each other. ---
examples: It took an hour to disentangle the fishing line.
She disentangled herself from the argument and left.
The two firms are still disentangling their finances.

entries.meaning: To spoil the appearance of a person or a thing badly. ---
examples: Graffiti disfigures half the buildings on the block.
The fire disfigured his hands.
The statue was badly disfigured by vandals.

entries.meaning: To make someone lose hope or confidence. ---
examples: Three rejections in a row would dishearten anyone.
The result disheartened the whole team.
She was disheartened by how little had changed.

entries.meaning: To bring shame on someone, or to refuse to honor an agreement or a check. ---
examples: Breaking that promise would dishonor everyone who fought for it.
The bank dishonored the check.
He felt dishonored by the accusation.
entries.contrast: American dishonor; British dishonour. The h is silent: dis-AH-nur.

entries.meaning: To show someone that what they believed in is not as good or true as they thought. ---
examples: I hate to disillusion you, but the job isn't glamorous.
Two years in politics disillusioned him completely.
Many young doctors are disillusioned with the system.

entries.meaning: To arrange legally that someone will not receive your property after your death. ---
examples: He threatened to disinherit all three children.
She disinherited her nephew in the final will.
The son was disinherited without any explanation.

entries.meaning: To force something or someone out of a fixed position. ---
examples: Use a stick to dislodge the ball from the gutter.
The storm dislodged several roof tiles.
The champion has not been dislodged in six years.

entries.meaning: To cut a body apart, or to break a country or an organization into pieces. ---
examples: The plan would dismember the company and sell the pieces.
The treaty dismembered the old empire.
The estate was dismembered and sold off in lots.

entries.meaning: To get down from a horse or a bicycle, or to take something off its mounting. ---
examples: Riders must dismount before crossing the bridge.
She dismounted and led the horse to the barn.
The lens had already been dismounted and packed away.
entries.русский: спешиваться, слезать (с лошади, велосипеда); снимать с крепления
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dismount the camera), intransitive (riders must dismount)

entries.meaning: To make someone lose their sense of where they are or what is happening. ---
examples: Bright lights and loud music can disorient you fast.
The fog disoriented even the local guides.
She woke up cold and completely disoriented.
entries.contrast: American English prefers disorient; British English usually says disorientate.

entries.meaning: To speak about someone or something as though they have little value. ---
examples: I don't want to disparage anyone's work here.
He disparaged his opponent at every stop on the tour.
Her research was disparaged for years before it was accepted.

entries.meaning: To make a feeling or a false belief go away. ---
examples: Let me dispel a few myths about the test.
Her calm voice dispelled the panic in the room.
The rumor was quickly dispelled by the photos.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: dispelled, dispelling.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone or make them unhappy. ---
examples: Any decision here is bound to displease somebody.
The tone of the letter displeased her.
He was clearly displeased with the result.

entries.meaning: To get rid of something, or to make someone inclined to feel or act a certain way. ---
examples: Please dispose of the packaging in the blue bin.
The court disposed of the case in a single morning.
She seemed disposed to give him another chance.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the news disposed him to accept), intransitive (dispose of the packaging)
entries.contrast: In the 'get rid of' sense it always takes of: dispose of the trash, never 'dispose the trash'.

entries.meaning: To take land, a home or property away from the person who owns it. ---
examples: The new law let the state dispossess absentee owners.
The war dispossessed millions of farmers.
Families dispossessed in the 1950s are still seeking compensation.

entries.meaning: To pay no attention to something, especially something you should consider. ---
examples: Please disregard the last email.
He disregarded every warning on the label.
The jury was told to disregard the remark.
entries.русский: игнорировать, пренебрегать; не принимать во внимание

entries.meaning: To insult someone or treat them with open disrespect, in informal speech. ---
examples: Don't diss the food before you've tried it.
He dissed her in front of the whole class.
She felt dissed by the way they announced it.
entries.contrast: Informal. The s doubles: dissed, dissing. Also written dis.

entries.meaning: To fail to give someone what they wanted or expected. ---
examples: A wait that long will dissatisfy even a loyal customer.
The settlement dissatisfied both sides.
Many employees are dissatisfied with the new schedule.
entries.contrast: Two s's in the middle, and the y becomes ie before -s and -d: dissatisfies, dissatisfied.

entries.meaning: To cut something open to study it, or to examine an idea part by part. ---
examples: We had to dissect a frog in biology class.
Analysts dissected every line of the speech.
The play has been dissected by critics for a century.

entries.meaning: To spread information widely to many people. ---
examples: The agency will disseminate the new guidelines next week.
The group disseminated the report to every member.
The findings have been widely disseminated online.

entries.meaning: To disagree openly with an official decision or a majority opinion. ---
examples: Two justices dissent in almost every case of this kind.
Only one board member dissented.
He has dissented from the party line more than once.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like descent (a way down) and close to decent (respectable). Usually dissent from.

entries.meaning: To separate one thing from another, or to declare that you have no connection with something. ---
examples: He tried to dissociate himself from the campaign.
The board dissociated itself from the remarks within an hour.
The two problems cannot easily be dissociated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dissociate the two questions), intransitive (the molecule dissociates in water)
entries.contrast: Also written disassociate with the same meaning, but dissociate is the standard form. Takes from.

entries.meaning: To persuade someone not to do something. ---
examples: Nothing I said could dissuade her.
His parents dissuaded him from dropping out.
He was not dissuaded by the price.
entries.contrast: The opposite of persuade, and it takes from + -ing: dissuaded him from going.

entries.meaning: To make it clear that you are not connected with someone or something. ---
examples: Politicians hurry to distance themselves from a scandal.
She distanced herself from the group's statement.
The brand has distanced itself from the old ads.
entries.contrast: Nearly always reflexive: distance yourself from something.

entries.meaning: To swell outward from pressure inside, or to make something swell that way. ---
examples: Too much air will distend the tissue.
Her stomach distended painfully after the meal.
The vet found a distended loop of intestine.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (gas distends the stomach), intransitive (her abdomen distended)

entries.meaning: To purify a liquid by boiling and condensing it, or to reduce something to its essential part. ---
examples: They distill the whiskey twice before bottling it.
She distilled three hundred pages into a single chart.
The findings have been distilled into one page.
entries.contrast: American English writes distill, British distil with one -l. Both double the l before -ed and -ing: distilled, distilling.

entries.meaning: To twist something out of its true shape, sound, or meaning. ---
examples: Cheap lenses distort straight lines.
The article distorted what she actually said.
His voice was distorted by the bad connection.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (distort the facts), intransitive (the sound distorts at high volume)

entries.meaning: To hesitate and delay instead of making a decision. ---
examples: Do not dither — the offer expires tonight.
The committee dithered for months over the budget.
While they were dithering, a rival bought the company.

entries.meaning: To separate and go in different directions, or to differ from something. ---
examples: The two trails diverge just past the bridge.
Their opinions diverged sharply after the vote.
Our careers had diverged long before graduation.
entries.contrast: Diverge takes from: the results diverge from earlier findings.

entries.meaning: To sell off a business or investment, or to strip someone of something they hold. ---
examples: The university plans to divest from fossil fuels.
The company divested its European division last year.
He was divested of his title after the scandal.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (divest its holdings), intransitive (divest from coal)
entries.contrast: Divest takes of when someone is stripped of something and from when an investor sells out: divested of his rank, divested from oil.

entries.meaning: To work out or guess something hidden without direct evidence. ---
examples: Analysts try to divine the bank's next move.
She divined from his tone that something was wrong.
No one has divined the author's real intent.
entries.contrast: Spelled and pronounced exactly like the adjective divine (божественный), but the verb means to guess something hidden.

entries.meaning: To reveal information that was supposed to stay secret. ---
examples: The company refuses to divulge the terms of the deal.
He divulged the password to a stranger.
Nothing has been divulged about the investigation.

entries.meaning: To change something dishonestly, especially a document, a photo, or a drink. ---
examples: It is a crime to doctor official records.
Someone doctored the photo before posting it.
The books had been doctored to hide the losses.
entries.contrast: Same word as the noun doctor (врач), but the verb means to tamper with something.

entries.meaning: To follow or trouble someone persistently. ---
examples: Money problems dog the project at every stage.
Injuries dogged him throughout the season.
The scandal has dogged the mayor for years.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the g doubles: dogged, dogging.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something certain to fail or suffer. ---
examples: One bad decision can doom an entire campaign.
The leak doomed their chances of winning.
The plan was doomed from the start.
entries.contrast: Doom takes to: doomed to failure, doomed to repeat it.

entries.meaning: To give someone drugs secretly, or to take banned performance drugs in sport. ---
examples: A few riders still dope to gain an edge.
The trainer doped two of the horses.
He admits he was doping all season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dope the horse), intransitive (athletes who dope)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dope → doped, doping.

entries.meaning: To mark something with dots, or to be scattered all over a surface. ---
examples: Small farms dot the valley floor.
She dotted the map with red pins.
The hills are dotted with wind turbines.
entries.contrast: One syllable, one vowel, one final consonant, so the t doubles: dotted, dotting.

entries.meaning: To fit together neatly with something else. ---
examples: Her research and his dovetail almost perfectly.
The new rules dovetailed with existing state law.
We are dovetailing the two schedules this week.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (the plans dovetail), transitive (dovetail the schedules)
entries.contrast: Dovetail takes with: the findings dovetail with earlier work.

entries.meaning: To knock something down, or to swallow a drink or food quickly. ---
examples: High winds can down power lines in seconds.
He downed the coffee and ran for the bus.
Three trees were downed by the storm.

entries.meaning: To make something seem less important or serious than it really is. ---
examples: Officials tend to downplay early warnings.
She downplayed her role in the discovery.
The risks were downplayed in the summary.
entries.contrast: Vowel + -y, so the y stays: downplays, downplayed, never downplaid.

entries.meaning: To reduce the size of a company or a household, usually by cutting jobs or moving somewhere smaller. ---
examples: Firms downsize when orders dry up.
The plant downsized twice in three years.
Her whole department was downsized last spring.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (downsize the staff), intransitive (the company downsized)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: downsize → downsizing.

entries.meaning: To vote against a post or comment online so that its score goes down. ---
examples: Readers downvote anything that looks like an ad.
Someone downvoted every answer in the thread.
His question was downvoted within minutes.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: downvote → downvoting. The opposite is upvote.

entries.meaning: To speak slowly, stretching the vowels out. ---
examples: People from that part of Texas drawl a little.
'Take your time,' he drawled.
She was drawling her words on purpose.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (he drawls a little), transitive (drawl an answer)

entries.meaning: To clear mud and silt from the bottom of a river or harbor, or to drag something up from it. ---
examples: The city plans to dredge the shipping channel.
Crews dredged the lake for the missing boat.
The harbor has not been dredged since 2009.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: dredge → dredging.

entries.meaning: To make a low continuous humming sound, or to speak in a dull monotonous voice. ---
examples: Air conditioners drone all summer here.
The engine droned for hours.
He was droning through forty slides.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: droned, droning.

entries.meaning: To bend or hang down from weakness, tiredness, or weight. ---
examples: The flowers droop if you forget to water them.
His eyelids drooped halfway through the lecture.
The flag was drooping in the still air.

entries.meaning: To give someone drugs, usually secretly, to make them sleepy or unconscious. ---
examples: Thieves sometimes drug a victim's drink.
Someone drugged the guard dogs.
She believes she was drugged at the party.
entries.contrast: One syllable ending in a single consonant, so the g doubles: drugged, drugging.

entries.meaning: To clean clothes with chemicals instead of water. ---
examples: You have to dry-clean a wool coat.
I dry-cleaned the suit before the interview.
The curtains are being dry-cleaned this week.
entries.русский: чистить в химчистке, отдавать в химчистку
entries.contrast: The verb keeps its hyphen: dry-clean, dry-cleaned. The shop is a dry cleaner's, two words.

entries.meaning: To fight or compete one against one. ---
examples: The two aces duel again tonight.
They dueled over the amendment for weeks.
The candidates have been dueling on television all month.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l — dueled, dueling — while British writes duelled, duelling. Sounds the same as the adjective dual (двойной).

entries.meaning: To make something less sharp, bright, or intense, or to become so. ---
examples: Two aspirin will dull the pain for a while.
The paint dulled after a single winter.
Years of routine had dulled his curiosity.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dull the pain), intransitive (the colors dulled)

entries.meaning: To astonish someone so much that they cannot speak. ---
examples: Results like that dumbfound the experts.
The verdict dumbfounded everyone in the courtroom.
She was dumbfounded by the size of the offer.
entries.contrast: The b is silent, as in dumb: dum-FOWND. The spelling dumfound also exists, but dumbfound is the usual American form.

entries.meaning: To trick someone into believing or doing something. ---
examples: Fake sites dupe thousands of shoppers a year.
He duped investors out of millions.
