They were duped into signing away their rights.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dupe → duped, duping.

entries.meaning: To make something else look small by comparison. ---
examples: The new tower will dwarf every building nearby.
This year's losses dwarfed last year's.
The stage was dwarfed by the size of the crowd.

entries.meaning: To blow something up with dynamite. ---
examples: Engineers had to dynamite the old dam.
They dynamited the roadblock at dawn.
The tunnel was dynamited shut.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: dynamited, dynamiting.

entries.meaning: To set money or resources aside for one specific purpose. ---
examples: Congress may earmark funds for rural clinics.
The city earmarked two million dollars for repairs.
That land has been earmarked for housing.
entries.contrast: Earmark takes for: earmarked for research.

entries.meaning: To move little by little in one direction, or to form a border along something. ---
examples: Prices edge higher every month.
He edged toward the exit without a word.
She was edging along the narrow ledge.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (edge toward the door), transitive (edge the lawn)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: edge → edging.

entries.meaning: To mix personal opinion into what is supposed to be a factual report. ---
examples: Reporters should not editorialize in a news story.
The anchor editorialized about the mayor for two minutes.
Critics said the paper was editorializing on its front page.
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ize; British writes editorialise.

entries.meaning: To bring something about, especially a change. ---
examples: Only Congress can effect a change this large.
The new director effected a complete turnaround.
Reforms have been effected at every level.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with affect. To affect something is to influence it; to effect something is to make it happen. Effect is usually the noun (эффект) and only rarely this verb.

entries.meaning: To supply something with electric power, or to excite a crowd suddenly. ---
examples: The state plans to electrify the whole rail line.
Her performance electrified the audience.
The village was electrified only in 1974.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: electrifies, electrified, but electrifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To kill or badly injure someone with an electric shock. ---
examples: A downed line can electrocute anyone who touches it.
The fault nearly electrocuted a technician.
Two workers were electrocuted at the site.

entries.meaning: To draw a response, answer, or reaction out of someone. ---
examples: Good questions elicit honest answers.
The ad elicited hundreds of complaints.
So far the letter has elicited no response.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with the adjective illicit (незаконный), which sounds almost identical.

entries.meaning: To make something longer, or to grow longer. ---
examples: Heels elongate the line of the leg.
The shadows elongated as the sun dropped.
The cells become elongated as they mature.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (elongate the shape), intransitive (the shadows elongate)

entries.meaning: To make something clear by explaining it carefully. ---
examples: The footnotes elucidate the author's sources.
She elucidated the theory with a simple diagram.
The paper has elucidated a mechanism no one understood.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (elucidate the point), intransitive (he declined to elucidate)

entries.meaning: To escape or avoid someone, or to stay beyond someone's reach or understanding. ---
examples: The right word can elude you for hours.
The suspect eluded police for a week.
The prize has eluded her three years running.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with allude (to mention indirectly): he alluded to the problem, but a solution eluded him.

entries.meaning: To come out from a source, or to give off a quality or feeling. ---
examples: Strange noises emanate from the basement at night.
A faint smell of smoke emanated from the kitchen.
The order turned out to have emanated from the mayor's office.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (light emanates from it), transitive (she emanates calm)
entries.contrast: Emanate takes from: the light emanates from a single bulb.

entries.meaning: To free someone from slavery, legal control, or restriction. ---
examples: The bill would emancipate minors at sixteen.
Lincoln emancipated the slaves in 1863.
She was legally emancipated at seventeen.

entries.meaning: To treat a dead body with chemicals so that it does not decay. ---
examples: Funeral homes embalm most bodies before a viewing.
The Egyptians embalmed their kings.
Lenin's body was embalmed and put on display.
entries.contrast: The l is silent, as in calm and palm: im-BAHM.

entries.meaning: To ban trade in something, or to forbid the release of news until a set time. ---
examples: Several states want to embargo the chemical.
Washington embargoed Cuban sugar in 1960.
The report is embargoed until Monday morning.
entries.contrast: Ends in -o, so the third person adds -es: embargoes, embargoed.

entries.meaning: To display a name, design, or slogan prominently on something. ---
examples: Teams emblazon the sponsor's name across the chest.
They emblazoned the logo on every window.
His face was emblazoned on a million posters.
entries.contrast: Emblazon takes on or with: emblazoned on the door, emblazoned with a crest.

entries.meaning: To be a clear example or physical expression of an idea or quality. ---
examples: Few leaders embody the values they preach.
That building embodied everything wrong with the era.
The rules are embodied in a single statute.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: embodies, embodied, but embodying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To press a raised design or lettering into a surface. ---
examples: They can emboss your initials on the cover.
The printer embossed the invitations in gold.
Each card is embossed with the bank's crest.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: embosses.

entries.meaning: To involve someone deeply in an argument or a difficult situation. ---
examples: One careless email can embroil a whole department.
The deal embroiled the firm in a two-year lawsuit.
He is embroiled in a fight with his own party.
entries.contrast: Embroil takes in: embroiled in a scandal.

entries.meaning: To act as the host who introduces the acts or speakers at an event. ---
examples: A local comedian will emcee the awards.
She emceed the benefit two years running.
He has been emceeing weddings since college.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (emcee the show), intransitive (he emcees for a living)
entries.contrast: Spelled out from the letters M.C. (master of ceremonies): emcees, emceed, emceeing.

entries.meaning: To show emotion openly, often in an exaggerated or theatrical way. ---
examples: Some actors emote far too much on camera.
He emoted through the entire second act.
She was emoting for the cameras.
entries.русский: бурно выражать чувства, играть с чувством
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: emoted, emoting.

entries.meaning: To mix two liquids that normally separate, such as oil and water, into one smooth blend. ---
examples: Whisk the oil in slowly to emulsify the dressing.
The sauce emulsified as soon as I added the yolk.
Keep emulsifying until it thickens.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (emulsify the butter), intransitive (the sauce emulsifies)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: emulsifies, emulsified, but emulsifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with love or admiration, most often used in the passive. ---
examples: The film tries to enamor the audience with nostalgia.
The city enamored her from the first day.
He is not enamored of the new schedule.
entries.contrast: American spelling enamor, British enamour. It usually appears in the passive with of or with: enamored of the idea.

entries.meaning: To express the essence of something briefly, or to enclose it in a protective shell. ---
examples: One photo can encapsulate an entire war.
Her answer encapsulated the whole problem.
The chips are encapsulated in resin.
entries.русский: кратко выражать, резюмировать; заключать в оболочку

entries.meaning: To cover or enclose something completely in a surrounding material. ---
examples: Builders encase the steel in concrete.
Ice encased every branch by morning.
The engine is encased in a soundproof box.
entries.contrast: Encase takes in: encased in glass. Drop the silent -e before -ing: encasing.

entries.meaning: To form a circle around something or someone. ---
examples: A high wall encircles the old town.
Troops encircled the city within a day.
The lake is encircled by pines.

entries.meaning: To put information into a code or a particular form, as in computing or genetics. ---
examples: The app will encode the file before sending it.
They encoded the message with a simple cipher.
This gene encodes a protein that repairs damage.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: encode → encoding. The opposite is decode.

entries.meaning: To include or cover a wide range of things. ---
examples: The term encompasses far more than software.
The survey encompassed twelve states.
The park was expanded to encompass the wetlands.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: encompasses.

entries.meaning: To move gradually into someone else's space, time, or rights. ---
examples: New subdivisions encroach on the forest every year.
Work encroached on every weekend that spring.
The desert has been encroaching for decades.
entries.contrast: Encroach takes on or upon: encroach on his rights. Third person adds -es: encroaches.

entries.meaning: To try hard to do something. ---
examples: We endeavor to answer every message within a day.
She endeavored to keep her voice steady.
They have endeavored to settle the case quietly.
entries.contrast: American spelling endeavor, British endeavour. It takes a to-infinitive: endeavor to explain.

entries.meaning: To drain someone of energy and strength. ---
examples: Long meetings in a hot room enervate even the most patient staff.
The humidity enervated the whole crew by noon.
She found the endless paperwork enervating.
entries.contrast: Enervate means to weaken, not to energize, despite how the word looks.

entries.meaning: To give a group of people the legal right to vote. ---
examples: The amendment would enfranchise residents of the territory.
A 1920 amendment enfranchised women nationwide.
Millions were finally enfranchised after the law passed.
entries.русский: предоставлять избирательное право, наделять правом голоса
entries.contrast: The opposite, disenfranchise, is far more common in the news: disenfranchised voters.

entries.meaning: To cause a feeling or a situation to come into being. ---
examples: Small kindnesses engender loyalty.
The mayor's response engendered real anger.
Years of secrecy had engendered deep distrust.

entries.meaning: To arrange something cleverly or secretly so that it happens. ---
examples: Lobbyists engineer deals like this behind closed doors.
He engineered a trade that saved the team's season.
The takeover was engineered by two board members.
entries.contrast: As a verb it does not mean to work as an engineer; it means to arrange something skillfully.

entries.meaning: To take up all of someone's attention. ---
examples: Puzzles like that engross him for hours.
The novel engrossed her so completely that she missed her stop.
He was engrossed in the game and never heard the doorbell.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive: be engrossed IN something.

entries.meaning: To order someone to do something, or in law to forbid an action by court order. ---
examples: Judges can enjoin a company from selling the product.
The court enjoined the state from enforcing the rule.
The agency has been enjoined twice this year.
entries.contrast: In American legal news it usually means the opposite of order: enjoin someone FROM doing something = forbid it.

entries.meaning: To make something more lively or more interesting. ---
examples: A few good questions enliven any lecture.
Her stories enlivened the long drive.
The old square has been enlivened by new cafes.

entries.meaning: To involve someone deeply in a situation that is hard to get out of. ---
examples: Bad loans can enmesh a family for years.
The scandal enmeshed three senior officials.
He is enmeshed in a lawsuit he never wanted.
entries.contrast: Usually passive: be enmeshed IN something.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something finer in character. ---
examples: Hard work does not automatically ennoble anyone.
The director claimed that suffering had ennobled his hero.
Volunteering there was an ennobling experience for the whole town.

entries.meaning: To settle someone comfortably or securely in a place. ---
examples: Cats ensconce themselves in the warmest spot in the house.
She ensconced herself in the corner booth with a book.
He has been ensconced in that office for twenty years.
entries.contrast: Nearly always reflexive or passive: ensconce yourself somewhere, be ensconced in a place.

entries.meaning: To preserve a right or an idea in a form that protects it permanently. ---
examples: Constitutions enshrine basic freedoms.
The treaty enshrined the right to appeal.
That principle is enshrined in state law.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive: be enshrined IN a law, a constitution, a charter.

entries.meaning: To make someone a slave, or to put someone completely under another's control. ---
examples: Debt can enslave a whole generation.
Colonial powers enslaved millions of people.
Their families had been enslaved for three generations.

entries.meaning: To catch someone or something in a trap, literally or figuratively. ---
examples: Cheap credit offers ensnare young borrowers.
The net ensnared a dolphin along with the tuna.
Two executives were ensnared in the investigation.

entries.meaning: To involve something as a necessary part or result. ---
examples: What exactly does this job entail?
The renovation entailed three months of noise.
The change has entailed a lot of extra paperwork.
entries.русский: влечь за собой, повлечь; требовать, предполагать

entries.meaning: To catch something in a tangle, or to involve someone in a complicated problem. ---
examples: Loose lines entangle propellers every summer.
The whale entangled itself in fishing gear.
He got entangled in a long legal fight.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's attention completely because something is so interesting or beautiful. ---
examples: Street magicians enthrall the tourists on the pier.
Her performance enthralled the whole theater.
The kids sat enthralled through the entire show.
entries.contrast: American English doubles the l: enthrall, enthralled, enthralling. British writing also uses enthral.

entries.meaning: To talk about something with obvious excitement. ---
examples: Fans still enthuse about that album.
She enthused over the new bakery for ten minutes.
He came back enthusing about the hiking trails.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the speech enthused the crowd), intransitive (she enthused about the trip)
entries.contrast: Enthuse ABOUT or OVER something. It is a back-formation from enthusiasm and stays informal.

entries.meaning: To attract someone by offering something appealing. ---
examples: Free shipping entices a lot of shoppers.
The store enticed customers with deep discounts.
He was enticed away by a better offer.
entries.contrast: Entice someone TO do something, or entice them INTO a deal.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with delight and wonder so that they cannot look away. ---
examples: Fireworks still entrance him at forty.
The dancers entranced the whole audience.
The children stood entranced in front of the aquarium.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the noun but stressed differently: the noun ENTRANCE (EN-truhnss) means a way in; the verb is in-TRANSS.

entries.meaning: To trick someone into doing something wrong, especially so they can be caught. ---
examples: Defense lawyers argue that agents entrap their clients.
The sting operation entrapped two dozen buyers.
He claimed he had been entrapped by an undercover officer.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the p doubles: entrapped, entrapping.

entries.meaning: To establish something so firmly that it becomes very hard to change. ---
examples: Tax breaks like these entrench inequality.
The reform entrenched the party's power for a decade.
Corruption is deeply entrenched in the system.
entries.contrast: Most often passive, with deeply: deeply entrenched habits, entrenched interests.

entries.meaning: To twist two or more things together, or to become twisted together. ---
examples: Wisteria vines entwine the porch railing every June.
She entwined her fingers with his.
Their careers have been entwined since college.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (entwine the ribbons), intransitive (the vines entwine)

entries.meaning: To name things on a list one by one. ---
examples: The contract enumerates every possible fee.
She enumerated her objections in order.
The report has enumerated six separate failures.
entries.contrast: No y-sound in American English: i-NOO-muh-rayt, not i-NYOO-muh-rayt.

entries.meaning: To picture something in your mind as a future possibility. ---
examples: We envisage a second location by next spring.
Nobody envisaged a delay this long.
The plan, as originally envisaged, cost half as much.
entries.contrast: Americans more often say envision; envisage is the more formal of the two and belongs to writing.

entries.meaning: To be a perfect example of a quality or a type. ---
examples: Those roadside diners epitomize small-town America.
Her first album epitomized the sound of the decade.
He has epitomized steady leadership for years.
entries.contrast: The noun is epitome, pronounced i-PIT-uh-mee — four syllables, not EP-i-tohm.

entries.meaning: To treat two things as if they were the same. ---
examples: Do not equate silence with agreement.
Critics equated the policy with censorship.
Speed is too often equated with skill.
entries.contrast: Equate one thing WITH another. The related noun is equation.

entries.meaning: To speak vaguely on purpose in order to avoid committing yourself. ---
examples: Politicians equivocate when the polling is bad.
He equivocated for twenty minutes and answered nothing.
She was still equivocating when the hearing ended.
entries.русский: говорить уклончиво, увиливать, уходить от ответа

entries.meaning: To make a mistake. ---
examples: When in doubt, err on the side of caution.
The clerk erred in the company's favor.
Having erred once, he double-checked everything after that.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say it like air; the older pronunciation rhymes with her. The everyday phrase is err ON THE SIDE OF something.

entries.meaning: To get away from a place or a danger. ---
examples: Most drivers escape with nothing worse than a fine.
The family escaped through a back window.
He has escaped serious injury twice this season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (escape punishment), intransitive (escape from prison)
entries.contrast: Escape FROM a place, but escape a fate with no preposition: escape from jail, escape punishment.

entries.meaning: To deliberately avoid doing or using something. ---
examples: Some chefs eschew salt almost entirely.
The band eschewed studio effects on this record.
She has always eschewed publicity.

entries.meaning: To publicly support a belief or a way of life. ---
examples: Few candidates espouse higher taxes openly.
The paper espoused reform for decades.
The values espoused in that speech were not new.

entries.meaning: To respect and admire someone or something greatly. ---
examples: Colleagues esteem her for her honesty.
Earlier generations esteemed thrift above comfort.
He is widely esteemed as a teacher.
entries.contrast: Usually passive in modern English: a highly esteemed colleague. The noun shows up everywhere in self-esteem.

entries.meaning: To praise someone highly, especially in a speech at their funeral. ---
examples: Old teammates still eulogize him at every reunion.
Her brother eulogized her at the service.
The founder was eulogized in every local paper.
entries.contrast: American English spells it -ize; British writing uses eulogise.

entries.meaning: To end an animal's life painlessly, usually because it is very sick. ---
examples: Shelters euthanize far fewer animals than they used to.
The vet euthanized the old dog that morning.
The horse had to be euthanized after the fall.

entries.meaning: To preach a faith to others, or to promote an idea with the same zeal. ---
examples: Startups hire people to evangelize the product.
He spent ten years evangelizing in rural Brazil.
The method has been evangelized at every conference since.
entries.русский: проповедовать; обращать в веру; активно продвигать (идею)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (evangelize a village), intransitive (they evangelize door to door)

entries.meaning: To show or prove that something is true. ---
examples: These numbers evidence a real shift in demand.
The letters evidenced a long friendship.
Support was strong, as evidenced by the turnout.
entries.contrast: In practice the verb is almost always passive: as evidenced by. The noun is uncountable — much evidence, never evidences.

entries.meaning: To take the heart out of something so that almost nothing useful is left. ---
examples: Budget cuts eviscerate the programs that actually work.
The amendment eviscerated the original bill.
The proposal was eviscerated by outside reviewers.

entries.meaning: To bring a feeling, a memory, or an image into someone's mind. ---
examples: Certain smells evoke childhood instantly.
The photograph evoked a summer she had forgotten.
His music has evoked comparisons to early jazz.

entries.meaning: To make a bad situation worse. ---
examples: Cutting staff now would exacerbate the backlog.
The drought exacerbated the food shortage.
Her injury was exacerbated by playing through it.

entries.meaning: To demand and get something from someone, usually by force or pressure. ---
examples: Storms like this exact a heavy toll on the coast.
The lender exacted a penalty for every late payment.
A high price has been exacted for that silence.
entries.contrast: Same spelling and stress as the adjective exact (precise), but the verb means to demand or impose: exact a toll, exact revenge.

entries.meaning: To praise someone or something very highly, or to raise them to a higher position. ---
examples: Sports writers exalt him every October.
The film exalted ordinary firefighters.
He was exalted to a rank he had not earned.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with exult (ig-ZULT), which means to rejoice. You exalt someone else; you exult yourself.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone very much. ---
examples: Automated phone menus exasperate everyone.
His constant excuses exasperated the whole team.
She was exasperated by one delay after another.

entries.meaning: To dig out earth, especially in order to uncover something buried. ---
examples: Crews excavate the foundation before anything else goes up.
Archaeologists excavated the site in the 1970s.
Only half the tomb has been excavated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (excavate a site), intransitive (they excavated for three seasons)

entries.meaning: To go beyond a limit or an expectation. ---
examples: Do not exceed the posted speed limit.
Sales exceeded last year's total by March.
The heat has exceeded every previous record.
entries.contrast: Only three common verbs end in -ceed: exceed, proceed, succeed. The rest are -cede (concede, precede).

entries.meaning: To take a short passage out of a longer text for separate use. ---
examples: Magazines often excerpt new memoirs before publication.
The paper excerpted two chapters last Sunday.
The passage was excerpted from her 2019 novel.
entries.contrast: The noun moves the stress to the front: an EK-surpt, but to ik-SURPT a book.

entries.meaning: To cut something out and remove it completely. ---
examples: Editors excise whole paragraphs when space runs short.
The surgeon excised the tumor.
Two scenes were excised before release.
entries.contrast: The tax noun is a different word with front stress: an EK-syz tax. And excise is not exercise.

entries.meaning: To officially exclude someone from a church and its rites. ---
examples: Few churches excommunicate anyone today.
The pope excommunicated him in 1521.
He had been excommunicated years before he died.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone very harshly in public. ---
examples: Editorial boards excoriate the plan every week.
The judge excoriated both attorneys.
He was excoriated in the press for weeks.

entries.meaning: To pass waste matter out of the body or out of a cell. ---
examples: Kidneys excrete most of the drug within a day.
The tree excreted a sticky resin all over the bark.
Salt is excreted through the skin when you sweat.

entries.meaning: To rub away dead cells from the surface of the skin. ---
examples: Dermatologists say you should exfoliate twice a week at most.
She exfoliated before putting on the mask.
Exfoliating too often can leave your skin raw.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exfoliate your skin), intransitive (the rock exfoliates in thin sheets)

entries.meaning: To make someone feel very happy and full of energy. ---
examples: Cold water and open sky exhilarate him.
The first run down the mountain exhilarated her.
We came home tired but exhilarated.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: ig-ZIL-uh-rayt. Note the spelling -hilar-, as in hilarious.

entries.meaning: To urge someone strongly to do something. ---
examples: Coaches exhort their players to finish every drill.
She exhorted the crowd to stay calm.
They were exhorted to give whatever they could.
entries.contrast: The h is silent and the x sounds like gz: ig-ZORT, like exhaust and exhibit.

entries.meaning: To dig up a buried body, usually for an official examination. ---
examples: Courts rarely order officials to exhume a body.
Investigators exhumed the remains in April.
The grave had been exhumed twice before.

entries.meaning: To force someone to leave their own country, usually for political reasons. ---
examples: Regimes still exile their loudest critics.
The junta exiled him in 1976.
He was exiled for writing against the government.
entries.contrast: Both EG-zyl and EK-syl are heard; the noun is spelled and stressed exactly like the verb.

entries.meaning: To be real or present in the world. ---
examples: Does such a thing even exist?
The company existed for less than two years.
Species have existed here for millennia.
entries.contrast: Never takes an object. The noun is existence, spelled -ence, not -ance.

entries.meaning: To drive out an evil spirit, or to get rid of a painful memory. ---
examples: Priests still exorcise houses in some towns.
The trip exorcised a lot of old guilt.
Those ghosts have never really been exorcised.
entries.contrast: Written exorcise or exorcize in the US, and pronounced almost like exercise — but the two words are unrelated.

entries.meaning: To make a process happen faster than usual. ---
examples: For an extra fee they will expedite the passport.
The clerk expedited our paperwork.
Shipping is being expedited for early orders.

entries.meaning: To use up money, time, or energy on something. ---
examples: Do not expend energy on arguments you cannot win.
The city expended most of the grant on repairs.
Half the fuel had been expended before they reached the coast.
entries.contrast: The formal word for spend, with the sense of using something up. The noun is expenditure.

entries.meaning: To feel or live through something. ---
examples: Most travelers experience some jet lag.
The region experienced its worst drought in decades.
Users are experiencing delays this morning.
entries.contrast: Spelled -ience: experience, not experiance.

entries.meaning: To explain an idea in detail. ---
examples: He will expound on that theory for hours.
She expounded her views at the town meeting.
The doctrine is expounded in chapter four.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (expound a theory), intransitive (expound on a topic)
entries.contrast: Expound ON a subject when there is no direct object.

entries.meaning: To take private property away from its owner, especially by government action. ---
examples: States can expropriate land for a highway.
The government expropriated the mines in 1938.
Their farm was expropriated without compensation.

entries.meaning: To remove something completely from a record. ---
examples: Some states let courts expunge juvenile records.
The judge expunged the arrest from his file.
The reference had already been expunged.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: expunging, not expungeing.

entries.meaning: To kill all the members of a group of animals or people. ---
examples: Store-bought poison will not exterminate a termite colony.
Settlers nearly exterminated the bison.
The nest was exterminated last week.

entries.meaning: To praise something very highly. ---
examples: Ads always extol the benefits and skip the risks.
She extolled the virtues of a small kitchen.
The program has been extolled by every reviewer.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: extolled, extolling. The base spelling extoll is old-fashioned.

entries.meaning: To use known facts to estimate something beyond them. ---
examples: You cannot extrapolate a national trend from one county.
They extrapolated next year's costs from the last three.
The forecast was extrapolated from incomplete data.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (extrapolate a trend), intransitive (extrapolate from the data)
entries.contrast: Extrapolate FROM known data TO a conclusion.

entries.meaning: To give off a quality or a liquid steadily. ---
examples: Good teachers exude calm on the first day of school.
The pine exuded sap all over the hood of the car.
She walked in exuding confidence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exude confidence), intransitive (sap exudes from the bark)

entries.meaning: To show great joy, especially after a success. ---
examples: Fans exult whenever that team beats the champions.
He exulted in the victory for a solid week.
The crowd was still exulting an hour later.
entries.contrast: Exult IN or OVER something. Do not confuse it with exalt (ig-ZAWLT), which means to praise.

entries.meaning: To measure or judge something roughly just by looking at it.
examples: I never measure the oil — I just eyeball it.
He eyeballed the gap and decided the couch would fit.
She was eyeballing the crowd for a familiar face.
entries.русский: прикидывать на глаз, оценивать на глазок
entries.contrast: Informal. It means to estimate by eye, or simply to stare hard at someone.
